note:
Dermatology follow-up on the ward, hospital day 3, for a 57-year-old male with moderate plaque psoriasis. He has been on secukinumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks for about a year and had good control until two months ago, when the plaques on his elbows and knees began to thicken and scale again. He admits to heavy alcohol use, about a pint of whiskey daily, and says his skin flares during his heaviest drinking weeks. He denies joint pain, morning stiffness, and fever. He reports he has not missed any secukinumab injections.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.4 F, heart rate 88, and blood pressure 132/84. On exam there are well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale over both elbows and both knees, covering roughly 6 percent of body surface area. There are no pustules and no nail pitting, and there is no sign of skin infection. The scalp is clear.

My impression is moderate plaque psoriasis, incompletely controlled on secukinumab and aggravated by heavy alcohol use. I will continue secukinumab 300 mg every 4 weeks and start betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment twice daily to the plaques for 2 weeks. A hepatic function panel will be sent today. I counseled him to cut back on alcohol, and I asked social work to arrange substance use counseling before discharge. He should return to dermatology clinic in 6 weeks.
summary: A 57-year-old male on hospital day 3 was seen for follow-up of moderate plaque psoriasis on secukinumab. Control was good until two months ago, when plaques on his elbows and knees thickened again, and he reports heavy alcohol use with flares during his heaviest drinking weeks. He denies joint pain, morning stiffness and fever, and exam shows erythematous plaques with silvery scale over about 6 percent of body surface area without pustules or nail pitting. The impression is moderate plaque psoriasis incompletely controlled on secukinumab and aggravated by heavy alcohol use. Secukinumab continues, betamethasone ointment is added, a hepatic function panel is sent, alcohol counseling is arranged, and clinic follow-up is set for 6 weeks.

note:
Nephrology progress note, hospital day 2. This is a 40-year-old male with CKD stage 3b from diabetic nephropathy, HTN, and T2DM who was admitted yesterday with hyperkalemia found on outpatient labs.

There were no acute events overnight. In the emergency department he received calcium gluconate 1 gram IV once and regular insulin 10 units IV once with 25 g of dextrose, and since then he has been on sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily. The admission ECG showed peaked T waves with a normal QRS duration, and the repeat ECG this morning was normal.

History was clarified today with the pharmacy fill record. He first told the admitting team that he takes lisinopril 20 mg daily, but the fill history confirms the dose is 40 mg daily, and 40 mg is the dose recorded in this note. He also told me that his copays have become unaffordable. He stopped furosemide about three weeks ago and has been stretching his insulin glargine, taking it only on most nights, because of the cost, while continuing the cheaper lisinopril. He has also been using a salt substitute made of potassium chloride since he was told to cut back on salt. He reports two days of fatigue and muscle cramps. He denies chest pain, palpitations, focal weakness, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He has no known drug allergies.

Home medications are lisinopril 40 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily (not taking), insulin glargine 20 units nightly (taken inconsistently), and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 78, blood pressure 148/92, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam he is comfortable with clear lungs, a regular rhythm, trace bilateral leg edema, no asterixis, and strength 5/5 throughout.

Data: potassium was 6.4 on admission and is 5.2 this morning. Creatinine is 2.1, up from his baseline of 1.8, with an eGFR of 38 and BUN 38. Serum bicarbonate is 19 and sodium is 136. Glucose is 210 and HbA1c is 8.9%. A renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

Assessment and plan by problem. Hyperkalemia, multifactorial from ACE inhibitor therapy, CKD, missed furosemide, and the potassium salt substitute, improving. Stop lisinopril and do not restart it for now. Restart furosemide 40 mg daily to promote potassium excretion. Continue sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily to complete 48 hours, then recheck a basic metabolic panel tomorrow morning. Stop the salt substitute, and the dietitian will teach a low-potassium diet. Mild AKI on CKD, likely prerenal from the ACE inhibitor and poor intake, improving; avoid nephrotoxins and trend creatinine daily. HTN is above goal off the ACE inhibitor, so increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. T2DM with cost-related insulin rationing: continue insulin glargine 20 units nightly, and social work and pharmacy will enroll him in a patient assistance program and move him to lower-cost formulary options before discharge. Continue atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He will follow up in nephrology clinic in one week with repeat labs.
summary: A 40-year-old male with CKD stage 3b, HTN, and T2DM was admitted with hyperkalemia, improved from a potassium of 6.4 to 5.2 after calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose, and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate. Because of cost he had stopped furosemide and rationed insulin while taking lisinopril 40 mg daily, a dose confirmed by the fill record after he first reported 20 mg, and he used a potassium chloride salt substitute. He denies chest pain, palpitations, and focal weakness. The assessment is multifactorial hyperkalemia with mild AKI on CKD, both improving. Lisinopril is stopped, furosemide is restarted, amlodipine is increased to 10 mg daily, and nephrology follow-up is in one week.

note:
Pediatric specialty clinic visit for a 2-year-old female brought in by her mother with two days of a barking cough. The cough began after two days of runny nose and has become worse at night, and her voice has become hoarse. Her mother has heard a noisy high-pitched sound when she breathes in while crying. She has had a low-grade fever up to 100.4 F at home, treated once with acetaminophen. She is drinking fluids and still making wet diapers. Her mother denies drooling, difficulty swallowing, vomiting, and any episodes of turning blue. She has not had a prior episode of croup. She has mild eczema controlled with emollients, and her immunizations are up to date. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination she is alert, playful, and in no acute distress. Temperature is 100.2 F, heart rate 128, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and weight 12.5 kg. She has a barky cough and a hoarse voice. There is mild inspiratory stridor only when she is agitated and none at rest. There are no retractions at rest, and her lungs are clear with good air entry on both sides. Her throat is mildly red without drooling, and both eardrums are clear. A rapid RSV swab is negative.

My impression is mild croup, a viral laryngotracheitis, with a low-grade fever and stable mild eczema. I gave dexamethasone 7.5 mg by mouth once in clinic, which is 0.6 mg/kg. She was observed for 30 minutes afterward with no stridor at rest. I advised acetaminophen 180 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever. I reviewed return precautions, including stridor at rest, drooling, labored breathing, and bluish lips, and I advised keeping her calm and offering plenty of fluids. Cough medicines are not recommended. Her mother will call if she is not improving in 2 days, and we will see her in clinic as needed.

Her mother denies drooling, difficulty swallowing, vomiting, and episodes of turning blue. On exam she had mild inspiratory stridor only when agitated, none at rest, no retractions at rest, clear lungs, and a negative rapid RSV swab. The impression is mild croup with a low-grade fever and stable mild eczema. She received dexamethasone 7.5 mg by mouth once, acetaminophen 180 mg every 6 hours as needed was advised, return precautions were reviewed, and her mother will call if she is not improving in 2 days.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. Please come in. I have you down as a 94-year-old female here with your daughter, and the concern is weight loss. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, that's right. I just don't seem to want to eat much anymore.
Family member: She has dropped from about 128 pounds to 112 pounds over the last six months. She lives alone and I come by every day. She skips lunch most days and picks at dinner.
Doctor: Is that how you see it, that you're just not hungry?
Patient: Well, yes, I'm just not hungry, and my dentures hurt my gums so I don't bother.
Doctor: Any trouble swallowing, or food getting stuck?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any vomiting, diarrhea, or blood in your stool?
Patient: No, none of that.
Family member: No fevers or night sweats either. She did say she feels dizzy when she stands up, though.
Patient: Yes, I get dizzy when I stand up too fast, mostly in the mornings.
Doctor: Have you fallen?
Patient: Not yet, but I've nearly gone down a couple of times.
Doctor: Let's go over your medicines. I see amlodipine and levothyroxine.
Family member: Amlodipine is 5 milligrams once a day, and levothyroxine is 50 micrograms every morning.
Doctor: And you have a history of high blood pressure and a thyroid problem?
Patient: Yes, I've had high blood pressure for many years, and I have an underactive thyroid too.
Doctor: Thank you. Here's what I found. Your weight today is 112 pounds. Your blood pressure sitting was 104 over 62, and standing it dropped to 90 over 56. Heart rate is 72 and oxygen saturation is 97 percent on room air. You walk slowly, and the timed up and go took 18 seconds. Your heart and lungs sound fine and your belly is soft and not tender. Your recent labs show a TSH of 2.4, which is normal, a hemoglobin of 11.4, which is a little low, and a creatinine of 0.8.
Doctor: So my impression is frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from poor appetite and sore dentures, and your blood pressure drops when you stand, which is orthostatic hypotension. The amlodipine is lowering your pressure too much, so I want you to stop amlodipine. Keep taking levothyroxine 50 micrograms every morning. I'll start mirtazapine 7.5 milligrams at bedtime to help your appetite and sleep. I'll refer you to a dietitian and to a dentist about the dentures, and we'll add nutritional shakes twice a day. Please come back in four weeks and we'll weigh you again.
Family member: That sounds good. Should we do any scans?
Doctor: Not right now. Given your goals, we'll hold off on invasive testing unless things change.
summary: A 94-year-old female came to geriatrics with her daughter for weight loss, with a drop from about 128 to 112 pounds over six months and a loss of appetite with sore dentures. She denies trouble swallowing, vomiting, diarrhea, blood in her stool, fevers and night sweats, but she feels dizzy when she stands up. Her blood pressure fell from 104 over 62 sitting to 90 over 56 standing, and her TSH was 2.4 with a hemoglobin of 11.4. The impression is frailty with unintentional weight loss and orthostatic hypotension. Amlodipine is stopped, levothyroxine continues, mirtazapine is started at bedtime, dietitian and dental referrals are made, nutritional shakes are added, and she returns in four weeks.

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. You're a 37-year-old female here for your COPD follow-up, correct?
Patient: Yes. I'm doing okay, but I've had more breathlessness lately going up stairs.
Doctor: How often are you needing your rescue inhaler?
Patient: About four times a week now. It used to be once or twice.
Doctor: And your daily inhaler, remind me what you take.
Patient: The umeclidinium-vilanterol, one puff every morning, and albuterol when I need it. I haven't missed any doses.
Doctor: Good. Have you had any flare-ups since I saw you last?
Patient: One, about four months ago. I got a steroid burst and an antibiotic from urgent care, and it settled in a week.
Doctor: Any coughing up blood, chest pain, or fever now?
Patient: No blood, no chest pain, no fever.
Doctor: Any swelling in your ankles or waking up at night short of breath?
Patient: No, nothing like that. I do cough up a little clear mucus in the mornings and I get wheezy when it's cold.
Doctor: You quit smoking about three years ago, right?
Patient: Yes, three years in March, and I haven't touched one since.
Doctor: Wonderful. And remind me, your alpha-1 antitrypsin level was low when we tested years ago?
Patient: Yes, that's why I got COPD so young.
Doctor: Right. Let me share what I found today. Blood pressure is 122 over 76, heart rate 82, breathing rate 16, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. On listening, I hear scattered wheezes and your breathing out phase is a bit prolonged, but no crackles. Your spirometry today shows an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted, and the FEV1 to FVC ratio is 0.58, which is a little lower than last year.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's a mild step down, together with the flare-up and needing your rescue inhaler more often. So my impression is COPD, moderate, not as well controlled as I'd like, related to your alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. I'd like to step you up to a triple inhaler. Stop the umeclidinium-vilanterol and start fluticasone-umeclidinium-vilanterol, 100/62.5/25 micrograms, one inhalation every morning. Keep albuterol, two puffs as needed. Rinse your mouth after each use. I'm also referring you to pulmonary rehab, and please get your flu shot this fall. Let's repeat the spirometry in three months and I'll see you then.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.
summary: A 37-year-old female with COPD related to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency came for maintenance follow-up, reporting more breathlessness on stairs and rescue inhaler use about four times a week. She had one flare-up four months ago and denies coughing up blood, chest pain, fever, ankle swelling and waking up short of breath. Exam showed scattered wheezes without crackles, and spirometry showed an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted. The impression is moderate COPD that is not well controlled. Umeclidinium-vilanterol is stopped and fluticasone-umeclidinium-vilanterol is started, albuterol continues as needed, pulmonary rehab is arranged, and spirometry is repeated in three months.

soap.assessment: COPD, moderate, not as well controlled as desired, related to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, with a recent flare-up and increased rescue inhaler use.

note:
Endocrinology telephone visit. Audio-only, no video, patient at home and verbally consented to the phone visit. This visit follows a hospitalization within the past month.

Reason for visit: follow-up of primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia in a 61-year-old male.

Interval history: He was hospitalized about three weeks ago with a left kidney stone and was found to have hypercalcemia. He was treated with IV fluids and ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy and was discharged after two nights. Since discharge he reports persistent fatigue, increased thirst, frequent urination, constipation, and bone aches in his hips and back. He denies confusion, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, flank pain, and blood in the urine. He takes calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily over the counter for bone health and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for hypertension. He is not taking any vitamin D.

Home measurements: blood pressure 128/78 and pulse 70 on his home cuff this morning.

Exam: no physical exam is possible by phone. His speech is clear, he is oriented, and he answers questions appropriately.

Data reviewed from the hospitalization and recent outpatient labs: calcium 11.6 mg/dL at discharge, PTH 88 pg/mL, 25-hydroxy vitamin D 22 ng/mL, and creatinine 1.1 with an eGFR of 72. A sestamibi scan showed uptake consistent with a right inferior parathyroid adenoma. DEXA showed a T-score of -2.6 at the distal radius.

Impression: primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia and a recent kidney stone, with osteoporosis at the distal radius, which meets criteria for surgery. Hydrochlorothiazide and calcium supplements are contributing to the elevated calcium.

Next steps: stop hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and stop calcium carbonate. Start amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. Start vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) 1,000 units daily for the low vitamin D. Drink at least 2 liters of water daily. Refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy. Repeat calcium, PTH, and creatinine in 2 weeks. I will call him again in 3 weeks. He verbalized understanding of the plan.
summary: A 61-year-old male with primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia was seen by telephone three weeks after a hospitalization for a left kidney stone. He reports persistent fatigue, increased thirst, frequent urination, constipation and bone aches, and denies confusion, nausea, vomiting and flank pain. Calcium was 11.6 mg/dL at discharge, PTH was 88 pg/mL, and a sestamibi scan showed a right inferior parathyroid adenoma. The impression is primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia, a recent kidney stone and osteoporosis, with hydrochlorothiazide and calcium supplements contributing. Both are stopped, amlodipine and vitamin D3 are started, he is referred for parathyroidectomy, and labs are repeated in 2 weeks.

note: Hospital day two progress dictation, orthopedics, on a 23-year-old male, correction, he is postoperative day one from open reduction and internal fixation of a right distal radius fracture with a volar locking plate. He fell from a skateboard two days ago and landed on his outstretched right hand. This morning he reports his wrist pain is about four out of ten and well controlled. Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 45-year-old male here for low back pain. Tell me what's going on.
Patient: It started about ten days ago after I moved some boxes at work. It's a dull ache across my lower back, worse when I bend or sit for long, and better when I walk around.
Doctor: Does the pain go down either leg?
Patient: No, it stays in my back. No numbness or tingling either.
Doctor: Any weakness in the legs, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, or numbness in the groin area?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or a fall or injury?
Patient: No fever, no weight loss, and no fall. Just the lifting.
Doctor: Have you taken anything for it?
Patient: Tylenol a few times, and some leftover muscle pills a friend gave me, tizanidine, but they made me so sleepy I couldn't drive.
Doctor: Okay. Any drug allergies I should know about?
Patient: Ibuprofen. It gave me hives and my lips swelled up years ago. So I stay away from Advil and Aleve too.
Doctor: Good to know. I've added ibuprofen to your chart as an allergy, so we'll avoid all of those anti-inflammatory pills. Let's review your regular medicines. You have diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux, right?
Patient: Yes. For the diabetes I take metformin 500 milligrams twice a day, losartan 50 for my blood pressure, atorvastatin at night, and omeprazole in the morning.
Doctor: Let me double check the doses against your record. Metformin 500 twice a day?
Patient: Hold on, let me look at the bottle. Sorry, I was wrong. It says 1000 milligrams twice a day. The 500 was my old dose.
Doctor: Thank you for checking. So metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, losartan 50 milligrams daily, atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night, and omeprazole 20 milligrams in the morning.
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 148/90, and on the repeat 146/92, heart rate 80, temperature 98.4 F, weight 238 pounds, BMI 33. Your A1c from last week was 7.4 percent, creatinine 0.9, and potassium 4.3. On exam you have tenderness and tightness in the muscles on both sides of the lower spine, no tenderness over the spine bones themselves, straight leg raise is negative on both sides, strength and reflexes are normal in both legs, and you walk normally.
Patient: So is it a disc problem?
Doctor: This looks like mechanical low back pain, a muscle and ligament strain, with no warning signs, so I don't need an x-ray or MRI right now. Your blood pressure is also above goal on both readings today, so your high blood pressure is not controlled, and your diabetes is acceptable with an A1c of 7.4 percent. Because of the ibuprofen allergy, no anti-inflammatory medicines. For the pain, take acetaminophen 1000 milligrams three times a day as needed, no more than 3000 a day. Stop the tizanidine and I'll start methocarbamol 750 milligrams three times a day for one week. Use heat, keep walking, and avoid bed rest. I'm also increasing losartan from 50 to 100 milligrams daily, and I'll recheck your potassium and creatinine in two weeks. Continue metformin, atorvastatin, and omeprazole as they are. Follow up in two weeks, sooner if you get leg weakness, numbness, or trouble with your bladder or bowels.
Patient: Okay, sounds good.

note:
Otolaryngology inpatient follow-up note, hospital day 3. A professional Spanish medical interpreter was used for the entire encounter, and the patient confirmed understanding through the interpreter. This is an 87-year-old male admitted with positional vertigo and a near fall, with a history of HTN, T2DM, atrial fibrillation, CKD stage 3, and BPH.

Through the interpreter, he describes brief spinning episodes lasting less than a minute that are triggered by rolling over in bed, looking up at a shelf, and bending forward. The episodes started five days ago and are accompanied by nausea. He denies hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, headache, double vision, facial droop, slurred speech, limb weakness, and chest pain. He first told me the vertigo had been present for about a month, but when the interpreter clarified the question, he explained that the spinning began five days ago and that the month-long symptom was only mild unsteadiness while walking. He also first stated that he takes metformin once daily; on further questioning, with the pharmacy list and the interpreter, the correct dose is metformin 500 mg twice daily.

Home medications reviewed are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly, and meclizine 25 mg three times daily, which he started from urgent care four days ago. He has no known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.0 F, heart rate 76 and irregular, blood pressure 136/78 sitting and 118/70 standing, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He did not feel dizzy on standing.

On examination he is alert and in no distress. Otoscopy shows clear canals and intact tympanic membranes bilaterally. Cranial nerves are intact, with no spontaneous nystagmus and normal extraocular movements. Finger-to-nose is normal, and he walks with a walker with a slow but steady gait. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right reproduced vertigo with an upbeating, torsional nystagmus lasting about 25 seconds that fatigued, and the left side was negative.

Data: MRI of the brain without contrast showed no acute infarct and mild chronic small vessel changes, and the CT head on admission was negative. Creatinine 1.4 with an eGFR of 47, sodium 138, potassium 4.2, glucose 142, HbA1c 7.2%, and hemoglobin 12.9.

Impression is right posterior canal BPPV. A central cause is unlikely given the normal neurologic exam and MRI. He also has an asymptomatic orthostatic drop in systolic pressure of 18 points that may contribute to his unsteadiness.

An Epley maneuver was performed on the right twice today. The vertigo and nystagmus resolved on repeat Dix-Hallpike afterward, and he tolerated it without nausea.

Recommendations: discontinue meclizine 25 mg three times daily, since vestibular suppressants delay compensation and increase fall risk at his age. Reduce amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg daily given the orthostatic drop. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly. Vestibular physical therapy consult and fall precautions. Teach home Brandt-Daroff exercises to the patient and his family through the interpreter using teach-back. Follow up in otolaryngology clinic in 2 weeks with an interpreter scheduled.

HD 2, hospitalist. 84-year-old female w/ LLE cellulitis, HTN, chronic venous stasis. Lives w/ daughter, ambulates w/ walker at baseline.
Admitted 2 days ago w/ red, warm, swollen L lower leg x 3 days.
NAE overnight. Afebrile. Leg pain improving, 5/10 -> 3/10. Eating well.
Denies fever, chills, purulent drainage, chest pain, SOB, calf pain.
Hx: no prior cellulitis, no DM, no PVD. Never smoker. Not on blood thinners.
Overnight RN: pain controlled, voiding well, slept okay, walked to bathroom w/ walker and 1 assist.

Meds: ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h. Amlodipine 5 mg daily. Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN. Lisinopril 10 mg daily on hold since admit (AKI). NKDA.

Vitals: Tmax 99.4 F, HR 82, BP 126/68, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA.
Exam: NAD, A&O. RRR, lungs CTA. L lower leg erythema, warmth, 1+ pitting edema; border marked on admit, receded ~2 cm from marked line. No bullae, no crepitus, no fluctuance, no purulence. DP pulses palpable. No foot ulcers.

Labs: WBC 14.2 -> 10.8. Cr 1.6 -> 1.2 (baseline 1.0). CRP 8.4. Blood cx x2 NGTD. LLE venous duplex neg for DVT.

A/P:
1. LLE cellulitis, improving on IV abx. Cont ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h today. If continues to improve, switch to PO cephalexin 500 mg QID tomorrow, total 7 days. Elevate leg, compression once infection settles.
2. Mild AKI on admit, prerenal, improving w/ IV fluids. Hold lisinopril. BMP in AM.
3. HTN, BP controlled on amlodipine. Cont amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Acetaminophen PRN for pain. PT eval. Dispo home w/ daughter likely in 1-2 days.
summary: An 84-year-old female with HTN and chronic venous stasis is on hospital day 2 for left lower extremity cellulitis. She is afebrile with improving leg pain and denies fever, chills, purulent drainage, chest pain, SOB and calf pain. The erythema has receded about 2 cm from the marked border, WBC fell from 14.2 to 10.8, creatinine improved from 1.6 to 1.2, and a venous duplex was negative for DVT. The assessment is improving LLE cellulitis with mild prerenal AKI and controlled HTN. Ceftriaxone continues with a planned switch to oral cephalexin tomorrow, lisinopril stays on hold, amlodipine and acetaminophen continue, and discharge home with her daughter is likely in 1 to 2 days.
